name: Russet-Vinaceous
lede: Russet-Vinaceous is a grayish reddish orange from Ridgway's 1912 plates that shares its exact hex with another library name, Clay Pink, one of at least eighteen near-duplicates filed under the same 1955 ISCC-NBS block.

sections.title: One hue, many names
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Nomenclature* plates this at hue 9‴ on plate XXXIX, and the Inter-Society Color Council's 1955 census files it in the same block, number 42, as a grayish reddish orange, Munsell 0.2YR 5.7/5.2 [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[cacao-brown]] and [[pinkish-brown]], at 
A shade warmer sits [[pinkish-brown]], about 3.9 units away, and [[clay]] a little further at 5.4 [1]. ColorHub's broader palette map also groups it near [[terracotta]], the nearest common design color, about 9.8 units off [1]. The name pairs *russet*, an old reddish-brown cloth color, with *vinaceous*, wine-colored, landing on a tan that leans more orange than either parent word suggests [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this reddish-tan in 326 of 23,781 paintings, 1.4 percent, as photographed [2]. It peaks in the 1400s, five times its average rate, and favors Pontormo, in 3 of his 13 dated works, and Paul Gauguin, in 5 of 50 [2]. Nepal's and India's paintings carry it far above the archive's base rate, nearly fifteen and eight times over [2]. The counts are a computed color match on varnished, photographed canvases, never a pigment identification [2].
